Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Bush condemned the escalated violence between Russia and U.S.-backed Georgia on Sunday, while Vice President Dick Cheney said aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." President Bush chats with Russian Prime Minister Vladmir Putin at the  start of the Olympic opening ceremonies. "My administration has been engaged with both sides of this trying to get a ceasefire," Bush told NBC's Bob Costas in an interview in Beijing, China, where the president has attended Olympic events. Bush was filmed speaking to Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin during Friday's opening ceremonies and said Sunday that he "was firm with Vladimir Putin" and that "this violence is unacceptable." Violence has continued to rage between Russia and the western ally since Thursday, when Georgia launched an operation to crack down on separatists in South Ossetia territory. Russia said it wanted to protect its peacekeepers already in South Ossetia following ceasefires in years past. But Georgia called it a full-on invasion. And while Russia has accused Georgia of a genocidal plot to cleanse the region of ethnic Ossetians loyal to Russia, Georgia accuses Russia of executing a long-planned war with the aim of taking control of the region -- including a key pipeline that carries Asian oil to Black Sea ports. "I expressed my grave concern about the disproportionate response of Russia," Bush said of his talk with Putin. "We strongly condemn bombing outside of South Ossetia." Putin says he's concerned about the flood of refugees arriving in Russia from South Ossetia. Russian officials said more than 30,000 refugees have left South Ossetia and crossed into Russia over the past two days, Interfax reported. "The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people," Putin said, according to Russian news agency Interfax. Meanwhile, Cheney talked to Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili on Sunday, telling him that Russia's aggression against Georgia "must not go unanswered." Cheney's spokeswoman Lea Ann McBride said the vice president spoke to Saakashvili to express "the United States' solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity." Georgia withdrew its forces Sunday and offered a ceasefire, which Russia refused. "The vice president told President Saakashvili that Russian aggression must not go unanswered, and that its continuation would have serious consequences for its relations with the United States, as well as the broader international community," McBride said. Saakashvili has called on the United States and the world community to stop the "intervention and invasion of my sovereign country." "I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world," he told CNN. "I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through." Two senior officials have told CNN the United States sent envoy Matt Bryza to the region to help with mediation.

“I expressed my grave concern about the disproportionate response of Russia,” Bush said of his conversation with Putin. “We strongly condemn bombing outside of South Ossetia.”

Putin said he was concerned about the flood of refugees arriving in Russia from South Ossetia. Russian officials said more than 30,000 refugees had left South Ossetia and crossed into Russia over the previous two days, Interfax reported.

“The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people,” Putin said, according to the Russian news agency Interfax.

Cheney’s spokeswoman, Lea Ann McBride, said the vice president spoke with Saakashvili to express “the United States’ solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

Georgia withdrew its forces Sunday and offered a ceasefire, which Russia refused.

“The vice president told President Saakashvili that Russian aggression must not go unanswered, and that its continuation would have serious consequences for its relations with the United States, as well as the broader international community,” McBride said.

Saakashvili has called on the United States and the international community to stop the “intervention and invasion of my sovereign country.”

“I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world,” he told CNN. “I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — President George W. Bush on Sunday denounced the worsening conflict between Russia and Georgia, a U.S.-supported ally, while Vice President Dick Cheney warned that Russia’s actions toward Georgia “must not go unanswered.”

Bush, who was in Beijing, China, to attend Olympic events, told NBC’s Bob Costas that his administration had been working with both Russia and Georgia in an effort to secure a ceasefire. The president had been seen speaking with Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin during Friday’s Olympic opening ceremony, and he said Sunday that he had been “firm with Vladimir Putin” in telling him that “this violence is unacceptable.”

Fighting between Russia and the Western-aligned Georgian government has continued since Thursday, when Georgia began a military effort against separatists in South Ossetia. Russia said its actions were intended to defend Russian peacekeepers who had been stationed in the region under earlier ceasefire agreements. Georgia, however, described Russia’s move as a large-scale invasion.

Russia has accused Georgia of trying to carry out a genocidal campaign against ethnic Ossetians in the region who are loyal to Russia. Georgia, in turn, has charged that Russia is carrying out a war planned well in advance, with the goal of seizing control of the area, including an important pipeline that transports Asian oil to Black Sea ports.

Bush said he told Putin he was deeply troubled by what he described as Russia’s disproportionate reaction. “We strongly condemn bombing outside of South Ossetia,” Bush said.

Putin has said he is worried about the large number of refugees entering Russia from South Ossetia. Russian officials reported that more than 30,000 people had fled South Ossetia into Russia over the previous two days, according to Interfax.

“The actions of the Georgian authorities in South Ossetia are a crime, of course, primarily a crime against their own people,” Putin said, as quoted by Russia’s Interfax news agency.

At the same time, Cheney spoke Sunday with Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and told him that Russia’s aggression against Georgia “must not go unanswered.” Cheney spokeswoman Lea Ann McBride said the vice president called Saakashvili to convey “the United States’ solidarity with the Georgian people and their democratically elected government in the face of this threat to Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

Georgia pulled back its forces on Sunday and proposed a ceasefire, but Russia rejected the offer.

McBride said Cheney told Saakashvili that if Russia’s actions continued, there would be “serious consequences” for Moscow’s relationship with the United States and with the wider international community.

Saakashvili has urged the United States and other countries to halt what he called the “intervention and invasion of my sovereign country.”

“I think the U.S. is the most powerful country in the world,” he told CNN. “I think the U.S. has lots of leverage. And I think there are lots of diplomatic means that it could be done through.”

Two senior officials told CNN that the United States had dispatched envoy Matt Bryza to the region to assist in mediation efforts.

counterfactuals.output:
**Bush condemns Russia’s military action in Georgia, warns of damaged relations**

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — President George W. Bush sharply condemned Russia’s military operations against Georgia during the conflict over South Ossetia, calling Moscow’s actions unacceptable and warning that they threatened a democratically elected government.

“Russia has invaded a sovereign neighboring state and threatens a democratic government elected by its people,” Bush said from the White House during the August 2008 crisis. “Such an action is unacceptable in the 21st century.”

The fighting erupted after Georgian forces moved into the separatist region of South Ossetia, where Russian peacekeepers were stationed. Russia responded with overwhelming force, sending troops and armor across the border and launching strikes deeper inside Georgia. Moscow said it was acting to protect Russian citizens and peacekeepers in South Ossetia, while Tbilisi accused Russia of a long-planned invasion designed to undermine Georgia’s independence.

Vice President Dick Cheney delivered one of the administration’s sternest warnings, telling Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili that “Russian aggression must not go unanswered.” Cheney said Russia’s military actions would have “serious consequences” for its relations with the United States and the broader international community.

Bush, who had cultivated a working relationship with then-Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin, said Moscow’s response was disproportionate and called on Russia to halt military operations, withdraw its forces and accept international mediation.

“Bullying and intimidation are not acceptable ways to conduct foreign policy in the 21st century,” Bush said.

Putin, however, defended Russia’s intervention and blamed Georgia for starting the war by attacking South Ossetia’s capital, Tskhinvali.

“Georgia’s actions in South Ossetia are, of course, a crime against its own people,” Putin said at the time, accusing Saakashvili’s government of using force against civilians and Russian peacekeepers. Russian officials argued that their military response was necessary to stop what they described as Georgian aggression.

Saakashvili appealed urgently for Western support, framing the conflict as a test of international resolve.

“This is not about Georgia anymore,” Saakashvili said. “This is about America, its values.”

The crisis placed Washington and Moscow on their most confrontational footing in years. The United States sent humanitarian aid to Georgia and pushed for a cease-fire, but ruled out direct military involvement. European leaders, led by France, helped broker a cease-fire agreement, though disputes continued over Russian troop withdrawals and the future status of South Ossetia and another separatist region, Abkhazia.

Russia later recognized both South Ossetia and Abkhazia as independent states, a move condemned by the United States, Georgia and many of their allies. Georgia and most of the international community continue to regard the regions as part of Georgian territory.

**Bush, in Beijing, Says He Pressed Putin Over Russia’s Military Action in Georgia**

**BEIJING —** President George W. Bush said Monday that he confronted Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin over Moscow’s military intervention in Georgia during a private conversation at the Beijing Olympics, telling reporters that the United States was “deeply concerned” by the escalating conflict and warning that Russia’s actions could damage its standing with the West.

Speaking from Beijing, where he attended the opening days of the Summer Games, Bush said he used a face-to-face meeting with Putin to urge Russia to halt its military operations and respect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. The conversation came as Russian forces moved beyond the separatist region of South Ossetia and as Georgian officials accused Moscow of carrying out airstrikes and widening the conflict.

“I was very firm with Vladimir Putin,” Bush said, describing the exchange as direct and serious. He said he told the Russian leader that the violence was unacceptable and that any attempt to topple Georgia’s pro-Western government or redraw borders by force would be met with strong opposition from Washington.

The crisis erupted after fighting between Georgian forces and separatists in South Ossetia, a breakaway region backed by Moscow. Russia responded with overwhelming force, sending troops, tanks and aircraft into the area and later striking targets elsewhere in Georgia. Moscow said it was acting to protect Russian citizens and peacekeepers in South Ossetia; Georgia accused Russia of launching a full-scale invasion.

Bush, who has cultivated a complicated relationship with Putin over the years, said the United States was working through diplomatic channels to press for an immediate ceasefire and a return to the pre-conflict positions. He emphasized that Georgia is a sovereign democracy and a close U.S. partner.

“There is no room for debate on this matter,” Bush said in substance. “Georgia’s territorial integrity must be respected.”

The president’s comments underscored the awkward backdrop of the Beijing Olympics, where world leaders gathered for ceremonies and diplomacy even as one of the sharpest confrontations between Russia and the West since the Cold War unfolded in the Caucasus. Bush and Putin were both in Beijing for the Games, giving the two leaders an unexpected opportunity to discuss the conflict in person.

U.S. officials said Bush also spoke with Georgian President Mikheil Saakashvili and other leaders as Washington attempted to coordinate an international response. The administration called on Russia to stop bombing Georgian territory, withdraw its forces and accept mediation. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice and other senior officials were engaged in talks with European allies, while U.S. diplomats pushed for action at the United Nations.

At the same time, the White House faced pressure to show tangible support for Georgia, a government strongly backed by Washington and a contributor to U.S.-led operations in Iraq. The Bush administration had supported Georgia’s aspirations to join NATO, a move fiercely opposed by Russia. The fighting threatened to deepen tensions not only between Moscow and Tbilisi but also between Russia and the United States.

Bush stopped short of threatening military action, and U.S. officials made clear the response would focus on diplomacy, humanitarian aid and international pressure. But the president warned that Russia’s conduct could have consequences for its relations with the United States and Europe.

“Russia’s actions this week have raised serious questions about its intentions in Georgia and the region,” Bush said, signaling that Moscow’s intervention could jeopardize cooperation on broader security issues.

The administration said it was also preparing humanitarian assistance for civilians affected by the fighting. Reports from the region described thousands of people fleeing South Ossetia and other areas as artillery, airstrikes and ground combat intensified.

Russia, meanwhile, defended its military campaign. Putin and other Russian officials accused Georgia of aggression in South Ossetia and said Moscow had a responsibility to protect civilians and Russian peacekeepers. Georgian leaders rejected that explanation, saying Russia had long sought a pretext to undermine Georgia’s government and reassert influence over the former Soviet republic.

The conflict placed Bush in a familiar but uncomfortable position: condemning Russian military force while acknowledging limited U.S. leverage. During his presidency, Bush had sought cooperation with Putin on counterterrorism and nuclear issues, even as relations deteriorated over NATO expansion, missile defense, energy politics and democratic backsliding inside Russia.

Now, with Russian troops operating inside Georgia, Bush cast the crisis as a test of the post-Cold War order.

“The days of intimidation and domination are not the way to conduct foreign policy in the 21st century,” Bush said in remarks reflecting the administration’s broader message.

As the fighting continued, U.S. officials called for international monitors and a negotiated settlement. European governments, particularly France, which held the rotating presidency of the European Union, moved to broker a ceasefire. Washington said it would support those efforts but insisted any agreement must include respect for Georgia’s borders.

The confrontation also reverberated through the presidential campaign back home. Candidates in both parties condemned Russia’s actions, with Republicans and Democrats alike calling for a tough response while avoiding direct military confrontation.

For Bush, the episode marked one of the final foreign policy crises of his presidency and a stark reminder of the limits of personal diplomacy with Putin. The two men had met repeatedly over nearly eight years, and Bush had once famously said he had looked into Putin’s eyes and gotten “a sense of his soul.” But in Beijing, amid the pageantry of the Olympics, the relationship appeared colder and more confrontational.

“I made my concerns very clear,” Bush said. “The violence needs to stop.”

The region fought a war with Georgia in the early 1990s and has since operated with de facto independence, backed politically and economically by Russia.
